@@91695275 <h> War has no grief scoreboard : Death in Israel and Gaza is not a sport <p> When you open the newspaper or scroll through articles online , you will see brief summaries of the war between Hamas and Israel . They might describe Hamas ' brutal invasion of Israel or Israel 's ferocious military response . They might provide some in-depth coverage about a particular individual , family , or town . Invariably , they will focus on numbers . <p> This number of Israelis have been killed , this number wounded , this number kidnapped , and this number released . This number of Palestinians have been killed , this number wounded , this number displaced . <p> Rather than focusing on cause and effect or the human impact of particular events ; rather than leading with compassion for civilians or seeking complexity and nuance ; rather than explaining the broader regional tensions that underlie the unfolding war , the news suggests that numbers tell the whole story . Whoever 's side suffers more losses wins the war of public opinion -- or at least a more favorable slant in the article . The larger the numbers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The death count has become a game of numbers , and spectators waiting to determine the winners and losers . But there are no winners in war , especially one that so painfully impacts civilians . The moment there are casualties or injuries -- physical or psychological -- everyone involved loses . And numbers can not adequately convey human pain and suffering . They obfuscate rather than clarify the losses inherent to war . <p> This is not a sporting event . There is no " 12th man " that can give one side home field advantage , and these are not video games with redos . Losses last a lifetime , and injuries to body and spirit endure . Yet we are enticed to engage war as a sport when news leads with a scoreboard , rather than human stories . We count losses and fouls , choose or reaffirm the sides we have taken , and absolve ourselves of the need to ask deeper questions about how the world can avert conflicts like this in the future . <p> Gamifying war takes the notion that " if it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Human life can not be summed up in a single data point . Doing so is deeply dehumanizing to those who have died , those who have been injured , and those who are in grief right now . Doing so erases their humanity in pursuit of personal gain . <p> In fact , Jewish tradition prohibits us from prioritizing numbers over people . Exodus 30:12 relates the formal prohibition of taking a census , even of the living : " When you take a census of the Israelites ... each shall pay God to redeem themselves that no plague may come upon them . " While it pertains specifically to ancient military service , our sages interpret this more broadly . The census depicts a group based solely on numbers , rather than on the human qualities of which it is comprised . It is therefore forbidden under most circumstances . <p> All the more so , we must stop desecrating the memory of the deceased and adding moral injury to those recovering from emotional and physical harm by grouping individual lives into simple figures . Doing so not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ongoing war , but also dehumanizes us as people far from the fighting and keeps us from empathizing meaningfully with those who do not have the privilege of geographic distance . <p> Hamas ' invasion of Israel and massacre of civilians was unspeakably brutal and dehumanizing . Israel 's military response has been incredibly painful for Palestinian civilians , as urban warfare reduces neighborhoods to battlefields . We risk diminishing our own humanity when we gamify this war or indulge ourselves by reading the news with an intense focus on numbers alone . <p> In our increasingly quantitative world , we rely on numbers , but they should not themselves be a headline -- much less a story unto itself or a way of understanding a complicated , unfolding war . But if statistics hide more than they reveal , we would do well to look beyond them . Now is the time for in-depth reporting on individual stories , which open our eyes to new perspectives and our hearts to all that we might not otherwise feel . <p> We risk closing our hearts when we focus on numbers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ adage that " a single life is like a whole world " -- a world of ideas , relationships , and creative potential . We should , instead , elevate the human stories that call us to compassion , grief , and empathy . May we pray and act to reduce not only the loss of civilian life , but also the loss of our humanity in the process of bearing witness to war . <p> Brodsky , a cantor , and Stanton , a rabbi , are co-clergy at East End Temple . Stanton is also director of leadership at the National Jewish Center for

" A major escalation could cause an initial surge in oil prices , with disruptive knock on effects on other commodity markets . " <p> Energy prices make up the majority of the World Bank 's commodity price index , so any price shocks would lead the whole index higher , it said . The commodity price index rose 5% during the third quarter , largely pushed by supply-side issues in oil markets , it said . <p> So far , the effect on markets have been muted , with oil prices pulling back after an initial shock , though they remain higher . Brent crude was trading at $88.11 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on Oct. 6 , the day before Hamas 's attack on Israel . <p> The bank highlighted previous Middle Eastern energy shocks , such as the Arab oil embargo in 1973 , the Iranian revolution in 1978 and Iraqi invasion of Kuwait in 1990 as instances when oil prices jumped on conflicts in the region . However , supply is much more geographically diverse now and in general the world is less reliant on oil compared to those periods , which could mitigate against some of the effects of conflict escalation , it said . <p> If oil prices do rise on the conflict , most other commodities including food and metals would also push higher , the report said . For example , higher demand for natural gas would push up the price of fertilizers , ultimately leading to higher food prices . <p> The Washington D.C.-based lender said it forecasts oil prices to average $90 a barrel this quarter , but also provided three price scenarios based on different levels of disruption to the market . <p> Under a small-disruption scenario , in which global oil supply is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ barrels a day , oil prices would initially increase by 3% to 13% or $3 to $12 a barrel above the baseline $90-a-barrel estimate . <p> Under medium disruption , oil supply could be cut by 3 million barrels a day to 5 million barrels a day . " This reduction would be comparable with the loss of 3% of global oil supply during the Iraq war in 2003 , " the bank said , adding that prices would initially increase by about 21% to 35% , or $19 to $31 a barrel , above the baseline . <p> If the war turns into a regional conflict , supply could fall by between 6 million to 8 million barrels a day--equivalent to the Arab oil embargo , leading to a 56% to 75% increase in prices , or an increase of between $50 and $67 above the baseline barrel price . <p> Gold prices could also rise on the conflict , as risk appetite from investors wanes and havens instead are sought , the bank said . The platform 's potential to rapidly disseminate easily downloadable and sharable content made it a crucial weapon . Hamas ' Telegram channels grew rapidly in the first five days of the conflict . @@103090262 <h> Hezbollah Hesitates as Israel Strikes Gaza <p> LONDON -- As Israeli troops move deeper south into the Gaza Strip with the goal of destroying Hamas , the world is closely watching what happens on Israel 's northern border , where its forces have engaged for weeks in intense clashes with another , more powerful foe , Hezbollah . <p> Hezbollah , the Lebanese militant group , has found itself in an awkward position since its ally Hamas launched a deadly , surprise attack on Israel on Oct. 7 . Now , after years of spoiling for a fight with Israel , Hezbollah is torn between maintaining its credibility as a defender of the Palestinians , and its hesitation to get involved in a full-scale war . <p> Throughout its 40-year history , Hezbollah has defined itself as a resistance movement dedicated to protecting Lebanon , battling Israel and backing the Palestinians ' quest for statehood . Yet after three days of Israeli ground incursions into Gaza and as the Palestinian death toll climbs over 8,000 , Hezbollah 's response has so far been worrying but restrained . <p> Hezbollah 's balancing act speaks to its outsize role in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ northern border . It is Lebanon 's most powerful political and military force , meaning that not even the Lebanese government can control its decisions , even when they affect the whole country . Hezbollah is also the most powerful node in a network of Iran-backed militias across the Middle East , which includes Hamas , meaning that its calculations often transcend Lebanon 's borders . <p> But as Israel 's air force levels whole swaths of Gaza , can Hezbollah maintain its reputation as a vanguard of the so-called axis of resistance movement if it sits on the sidelines of the conflict ? <p> Hezbollah 's last major war with Israel was in 2006 , and the group now has more sophisticated weapons and cadres of battle-hardened militants than it had then . But so far , it has engaged only in limited skirmishes with Israeli troops . It could squeeze Israel by expanding its attacks on the country 's north while a large part of the Israeli military is tied up in Gaza , Western and Arab officials say , but for now the group is holding back @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , there is little appetite for war , as the country suffers through a crippling economic crisis . But will Israel start a war ? We need equal pressure on them , too .
